Subject: Clarification on FX Exposure Assessment for FY26 Cross-border Settlements

First, I want to confirm our understanding of your team’s position: you believe the 3.2% average FX fluctuation range for HK$ settled cross-border transactions in 9M26 should be fully incorporated into the target company’s net working capital adjustments.

Our team’s analysis is based on the company’s actual hedging records from FY24 and FY25, which show only 0.8% of total cross-border transactions were covered by forward contracts, with the remaining 99.2% exposed to unhedged spot rate moves. We also noted that the company’s internal policy only requires hedging for transactions exceeding USD 500,000, which covers less than 15% of their monthly cross-border settlement volume.

To align our positions moving forward, we suggest we jointly review the company’s 20 most recent unhedged settlement batches by end of day Thursday, so we can finalize a consistent assessment approach before the Friday deadline.

Subject: Query on Compliance of Social Insurance and Housing Fund Contribution Bases for FY24 and FY25

Dear Ms. Li,

This email follows up on the data collection for the FDD project of XYZ Manufacturing Co., Ltd., and we wish to flag a discrepancy identified in the social insurance and housing fund contribution records we received on October 12, 2026.

Upon cross-referencing the provided contribution statements with the company’s payroll ledgers and individual income tax filing records for FY24 and FY25, we found that the declared contribution bases for 72 frontline production employees in Q3 FY24, 61 technical support staff in Q2 FY25 and 48 senior operators in Q4 FY25 are RMB 1,200 lower than their actual monthly taxable income as reported to the tax bureau.

We have attached a summary sheet that lists each affected employee’s department, payroll period, reported contribution base, and the verified actual income for your reference. Please note that this is not a comprehensive audit of all contribution records, but a spot check based on the sample data we have received so far.

To clarify the situation and complete our verification work, we request that you provide the full monthly social insurance and housing fund contribution declarations for all employees for the full FY24 and FY25 periods, along with the corresponding payroll reconciliation reports that link contribution bases to actual monthly compensation.

Please share these documents via the secure project portal by October 27, 2026. If you have any questions about the identified discrepancy or the required materials, feel free to reach out to me at your convenience.

Best regards,
Zhang Wei
Senior FDD Project Manager

Subject: FDD Finding: Non-compliant Supplier Rebate Accounting

This finding identifies a material misstatement in the target’s FY24 to 9M26 supplier rebate accounting, with a total recorded but unadjusted impact of RMB 12.87 million. The team failed to recognize accrued rebate liabilities when goods were received, instead booking rebate income only when cash refunds were received in the following period.

We verified this discrepancy by cross-referencing 21 signed rebate agreements with the general ledger and supporting payment records. For example, under the Q3 FY25 agreement with Shanghai Hardware Co., the target accrued RMB 892,000 in rebates in September 2025 but only recorded the income when the refund was received in October 2025, violating ASC 606 revenue recognition rules. A similar delay was found across 17 of the 21 sampled agreements.

The identified misstatement only applies to accrual-based rebate arrangements, not one-time cash discounts settled at the time of purchase. The impact excludes FY23 data and the partial 10M26 rebate claims that have not yet been submitted by suppliers, so the full FY26 impact may be up to 15% higher than the current quantified amount.

Subject: Analysis of Accounts Receivable Aging and Bad Debt Policy Mismatch for Target Co.

This report summarizes the misalignment between the target company’s accounts receivable aging structure and its stated bad debt recognition policy, based on FY24, FY25 and 9M26 financial data. Over the past two fiscal years and the first nine months of 2026, the company’s reported bad debt reserve ratios have stayed consistently below 1.2%, while its aging profile has shifted toward longer overdue balances. This initial contrast signals a potential under-provisioning risk that warrants closer review.

Breaking down the aging trends first, the share of receivables overdue by more than 90 days rose from 8.3% of total receivables in FY24 to 11.7% in FY25, and further jumped to 15.2% in 9M26. Over the same period, the share of current receivables (due within 30 days) fell from 62.1% to 54.8% and then to 49.3%, showing a clear deterioration in the quality of the company’s trade receivables.

The company’s official bad debt policy states that it will recognize a 5% reserve for receivables overdue 31–60 days, 10% for 61–90 days, and 20% for balances overdue over 90 days. Applying this policy to the 9M26 aging data shows that the required reserve should total 3.8% of total receivables, compared to the 1.1% the company actually recorded in its latest financial statements.

This gap between required and recorded reserves translates to a RMB 21.7 million under-provisioned bad debt expense for 9M26 alone, based on the total receivables balance of RMB 1.24 billion as of September 30, 2026. Even using a simplified average of the prior two years’ reserve ratios, the required provision would still be more than double the reported amount, highlighting the consistency of the mismatch over time.

The mismatch does not appear to be a one-time adjustment error, as the trend has worsened quarter over quarter in 2026, with the 15.2% overdue over 90 days balance marking a 3.5 percentage point increase from FY25’s full-year figure. This sustained shift means the current reserve policy is no longer aligned with the company’s actual receivables performance, creating a material risk to reported profitability in future reporting periods.

This analysis is limited to the publicly disclosed aging and policy data, and further review of customer payment history and internal collection records would be needed to confirm the full extent of the reserve shortfall and its impact on the target’s valuation.

Subject: FY24-FY25 Target Company Related Party Loan Due Diligence Executive Summary

The target company’s related party cash lending business carries unpriced credit risk that exceeds industry benchmarks for peer firms. During FY24 and FY25, the company extended RMB 890 million and RMB 1.12 billion in unsecured loans to its controlling shareholder’s operating subsidiaries, with no formal interest rate agreements signed for 62% of these advances. Unlike local manufacturing peers that charge an average 4.2% annual interest on related party loans, the target company only recognized interest income of 1.8% on these balances in FY25, resulting in an estimated RMB 27 million in unrecorded interest revenue last year.

The lack of standardized loan documentation creates material compliance and enforceability risks for the target company. Of the 14 related party loan agreements reviewed during the engagement, only 3 included fixed repayment schedules and clear default clauses, while the remaining 11 were drafted as informal internal fund transfers with no明确期限或违约责任条款. In the event of the controlling shareholder’s liquidity stress, the company would have limited legal recourse to recover these outstanding balances, which totaled RMB 1.05 billion as of 30 September 2026.

The current tracking and reporting of related party loans is inconsistent with the target company’s public disclosure requirements. The company’s internal financial system only logs monthly outstanding balances, with no tracking of individual loan terms, repayment progress, or accrued interest calculations. This gap means the board and external auditors have received incomplete and misleading periodic updates on the company’s related party transaction exposure over the past two fiscal years.

Subject: FY26 Valuation Impact of Seasonal Working Capital Normalization

This note outlines the seasonal working capital normalization adjustment applied to the target’s FY26 forecasted financials, as requested in yesterday’s FDD kickoff meeting. The adjustment addresses the target’s consistent Q3 and Q4 inventory build-up, which distorts quarterly working capital ratios and creates misleading near-term valuation signals for FY26.

We defined the normalization baseline as the average quarterly working capital turnover ratio across FY24 and FY25, excluding the distorted Q3 and Q4 periods of those two fiscal years. For FY24, the adjusted quarterly turnover was 2.1x for Q1 and Q2, and 2.0x for Q1 and Q2 of FY25, with a weighted average of 2.05x applied to the FY26 forecast.

Using this baseline, we calculated the normalized working capital balance for FY26 as RMB 128 million, compared to the unadjusted forecasted working capital of RMB 162 million. This represents a RMB 34 million reduction in gross working capital requirements for the 12-month forecast period.

Since the target uses an EV/EBITDA multiple of 8.2x for FY26 as agreed in the initial valuation framework, the RMB 34 million working capital adjustment translates directly to a RMB 34 million increase in enterprise value. We verified this calculation by cross-referencing the quarterly working capital projections against the target’s historical inventory turnover trends from 9M26 data shared last week.

We have included a detailed breakdown of the quarterly adjustment calculations in the attached FDD valuation workbook, and welcome any questions or feedback on the methodology or impact numbers prior to our final review this Friday.

Subject: Caveat on Accounts Receivable Aging and Bad Debt Policy Alignment for FY24-9M26

For the FDD engagement for XYZ Manufacturing acquisition, we have completed a high-level review of the group’s reported accounts receivable (AR) balance as of 30 September 2026, which totaled RMB 1.28 billion across 12 operating subsidiaries. We cross-referenced the reported aging buckets—0-30 days, 31-90 days, 91-180 days, and over 180 days—against the group’s formal bad debt policy, which reserves 0%, 5%, 20%, and 50% of outstanding balances for each respective bucket.

Our initial check found that 8 out of the 12 subsidiaries did not align their aging tracking with the policy’s required bucket definitions. For example, two subsidiaries categorized all balances overdue by 31-120 days into a single 31-90 day bucket, while three others omitted the 91-180 day aging tier entirely from their internal reporting systems.

We requested full, subsidiary-level AR aging breakdowns with customer-level details on 12 October 2026, and as of 15 October 2026, we have only received consolidated summary data from the group’s headquarters. We have not been able to verify the accuracy of the reported aging tiers for individual subsidiaries due to this missing granular data.

This gap in supporting documentation means we cannot confirm whether the group’s reported bad debt reserve balances for FY24 and 9M26 are calculated in compliance with its stated policy. Specifically, we cannot assess whether the 8 non-compliant subsidiaries underreserved or overreserved funds relative to their actual overdue AR balances.

We will update our analysis and finalize the AR-related findings once we receive the detailed subsidiary-level aging reports, and we will note any material adjustments to our draft report at that time. Until then, this caveat applies to all AR-related sections of the current FDD deliverable.

Subject: Escalation: Unresolved FY25/FY26F Cost Allocation Methodology for Project Spin-off.

We require your immediate guidance on the unresolved shared cost allocation methodology between Entity A and Entity B for FY25 and FY26F. Despite our three technical discussions with the Seller’s finance team over the past two weeks, they insist on using headcount as the sole driver for IT and HR shared costs. Our preliminary analysis indicates that this headcount-based approach does not reflect the actual resource consumption of the respective businesses.

This methodological disagreement has a material impact on the target's carve-out financial statements, shifting significant expenses between entities. Applying the Seller's headcount driver increases FY25 carve-out operating expenses by RMB 12.4 million compared to our activity-based costing approach, which utilizes actual system transaction volume. Consequently, the target's projected FY26F EBITDA margin would decrease by 4.2 percentage points, dropping from 15.5% under our proposed model to 11.3% under the Seller's current proposal.

To finalize the FDD report for the upcoming steering committee meeting on Friday, we need your decision on whether to accept the Seller’s headcount methodology with a formal disclosure of the valuation risk, or to formally escalate this to the Seller's CFO for a revised revenue-based compromise. We have prepared a sensitivity analysis comparing both allocation methods in the draft report appendix for your immediate review. Please let us know how you would like to proceed by 5:00 PM today.

structure.why: 开门见山提出需要合伙人决策的问题，交代背景（经过3次沟通无果）以证明项目组已尽力尝试，并非轻易放弃。

Subject: Caveat on R&D Capitalization Assessment for 9M26

This memorandum outlines the scope and limitations of our review of the target company’s R&D capitalization practices for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (9M26). We have cross-referenced the company’s disclosed R&D expenditure line items in its FY23, FY24, FY25 and 9M26 financial statements, and verified the matching internal project approval documents and capitalization eligibility checklists for 32 identified R&D projects.

We have not conducted independent on-site interviews with the company’s core R&D technical team, nor have we obtained third-party validation reports from external patent agencies or industry experts to confirm the technical feasibility of the 14 ongoing projects in 9M26. This gap arises because the company restricted access to external collaboration records and requested that no third-party outreach be initiated during the review period.

Based on our verified internal documentation, we have confirmed that 18 of the 32 reviewed projects met the company’s self-stated capitalization criteria during 9M26, with a total capitalized R&D cost of RMB 128.7 million. However, we cannot confirm whether these projects would meet the mandatory disclosure standards required by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) for public listed companies, as we did not access the latest CSRC regulatory updates released in October 2026.

The unvalidated technical feasibility of the 14 ongoing projects could lead to a material misstatement of the capitalized R&D balance if the company’s internal eligibility criteria are not aligned with prevailing regulatory expectations. Additionally, the omission of CSRC’s 2026 regulatory changes may cause our assessment to understate the required adjustments to the target’s reported R&D figures.

This caveat is intended to clarify that our review is limited to the internal records provided by the target company, and our conclusions do not constitute a formal opinion on compliance with external regulatory requirements or third-party validation of project viability.

Subject: FDD Exec Summary: Lease Classification Risks for Retail Target FY26

89% of the target’s 127 active retail store leases were misclassified as operating leases in FY25, which will overstate reported EBITDA by approximately RMB 21.7 million for the full fiscal year. The misclassification stems from the target’s failure to identify embedded purchase options and 7+ year residual value guarantees in 32 of the sampled mall-based leases. Our audit team verified that these terms meet IFRS 16 criteria for finance lease classification per the sample test results.

The overstatement of FY25 EBITDA represents 12% of the target’s originally disclosed pre-tax profit, which could trigger material adverse change clauses in the preliminary sale and purchase agreement. We identified 19 leases where the target has already recorded right-of-use assets but omitted corresponding lease liabilities, creating a RMB 8.3 million balance sheet misstatement as of 30 September 2026.

We recommend the deal team request a full lease classification review within 5 business days to quantify the full FY26 impact and update the target’s financial forecasts. Delaying this review could push the closing timeline by at least 2 weeks and increase the risk of post-closing audit adjustments.

items.en:
The impact of one-time government grants on reported recurring EBITDA has shifted notably across the three fiscal years we analyzed. Most recently, FY26F projections show the largest proportional distortion of the three-year period, with the grant set to account for 12% of headline EBITDA compared to just 4% in FY24. This shift stems from a planned strategic investment grant tied to the target’s new regional production hub, which was not included in prior year disclosures. 

To frame this adjustment clearly, we first define the scope of the grants we are excluding from recurring EBITDA calculations. All grants classified as non-operating, one-time income under IFRS 20 are excluded, including the FY25 factory modernization grant and the FY26 regional expansion grant. We have retained only recurring operational subsidies tied to ongoing workforce training programs, which represent less than 1% of total EBITDA in all reported periods. 

The most significant trend emerges when comparing the year-over-year change in grant size relative to core EBITDA. In FY24, the one-time grant totaled RMB 8.7 million, while core EBITDA came in at RMB 217.5 million. By FY25, the grant had grown to RMB 11.2 million, but core EBITDA rose to RMB 268.3 million, keeping the distortion relatively contained. The FY26F projection sees core EBITDA dip slightly to RMB 259.1 million, paired with a grant of RMB 35.2 million, creating the sharp imbalance. 

This imbalance carries meaningful implications for how investors and acquirers will value the target company. Many market participants use trailing 12-month EBITDA as a core valuation metric, and an unadjusted FY26F figure would overstate recurring operating performance by a material margin. Without proper normalization, the target’s implied valuation multiple would be roughly 10% lower than it would appear at first glance to analysts unfamiliar with the grant structure. 

We have included a full breakdown of grant values and core EBITDA figures in the attached appendix, alongside a standardized adjustment template for the diligence team to use across all comparable targets. This template will help ensure consistent treatment of one-time subsidies across every phase of the FDD process, reducing the risk of misaligned valuation conclusions among team members. 

Finally, we recommend flagging this adjustment in the final diligence report with a clear note on its proportional impact, so all stakeholders can evaluate the target’s underlying operational performance free from the distortion of temporary government support.

Subject: Follow-up on Lease Classification Dispute for FY25 Audit

First, I would like to confirm that I fully understand your team’s position on the lease classification for the 12 office spaces leased across three regional offices in FY25. You have determined that all 12 agreements qualify as operating leases, based on the criterion that none of the contracts grant our client a purchase option at a price below fair market value, and the lease term accounts for 62% of the total useful life of the assets, which falls just below the 75% bright-line threshold under IFRS 16.

Based on our review of the same lease agreements and supporting documents, our team has identified two key points that lead to a different classification conclusion. First, the lease for the Shanghai regional office includes a contingent rent clause tied to the client’s monthly revenue exceeding RMB 2.8 million, which we interpret as a variable payment tied to the underlying asset’s performance, rather than a purely fixed operating lease payment. Second, the lessor retains no substantive residual value guarantees for any of the 12 leases, and our client will take over full maintenance responsibilities for all assets starting from the 18th month of each contract.

We have cross-referenced our analysis with the latest Q1 2026 IFRS 16 implementation guidance issued by the International Accounting Standards Board, which clarifies that contingent rent tied to asset performance should be considered when evaluating whether a lease transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership. Additionally, the maintenance responsibility transfer shifts the majority of operational risks to our client, which is a supplementary indicator of lease classification under the standard.

To align our teams on this matter, we propose scheduling a 30-minute sync call next Tuesday, April 15, 2026, to walk through our detailed working papers and compare our respective interpretations of the relevant criteria. We can share our annotated lease agreement summaries and calculation spreadsheets via secure file transfer by Monday afternoon to ensure both teams have sufficient time to review prior to the call.

We recognize that this interpretation differs from your initial assessment, and we are committed to working collaboratively to resolve this discrepancy in line with the applicable accounting standards, rather than delaying the audit timeline for the FY25 financial statements.

Subject: Query on Inventory Impairment Provision for FY24 and FY25

This email is to follow up on discrepancies identified during our financial due diligence review of your company’s inventory impairment provisions for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. During our sample testing of 12 finished goods SKUs across three product lines, we found that your recorded impairment reserves totaled RMB 8.2 million for FY24 and RMB 9.7 million for FY25, while our independent valuation of the same SKUs indicated required reserves of RMB 15.1 million and RMB 17.4 million respectively.

To support our reconciliation of these differences, we request that you provide the following specific documents by Friday, 18 April 2026: the detailed inventory aging report for each tested SKU as of 31 December 2024 and 31 December 2025, the third-party valuation reports used to calculate your original impairment provisions, and the board minutes approving the initial reserve amounts for both fiscal years.

We understand that your team has been busy with year-end closing and annual reporting, but timely submission of these materials will help us finalize our FDD report without further delays. Please let us know if you need additional clarification on our testing methodology or the specific SKUs included in our sample.

Best regards,
[Your Full Name]
FDD Audit Team

Subject: FY24-FY25 9M Social Insurance and Housing Fund Compliance Finding

This finding documents a material non-compliance with local social insurance and housing fund contribution requirements for the target company during FY24 and the first nine months of FY25.

During our review of payroll records and official contribution filings, we identified that the company underreported the monthly contribution base for 82% of its full-time employees across all regional subsidiaries. For eligible employees, the actual reported base averaged 68% of their total taxable compensation, compared to the mandatory 100% requirement under local regulations.

The total underpaid contribution amount for FY24 is RMB 12.78 million, and for the first nine months of FY25, the figure stands at RMB 9.42 million. These figures represent the gross estimated shortfall based on the difference between reported bases and the required full taxable compensation, without accounting for any potential penalty waivers or administrative adjustments.

We verified this finding by cross-referencing three sets of documents: the company’s internal payroll ledgers for each subsidiary, the official social insurance and housing fund contribution receipts issued by local authorities, and the annual employee bonus and allowance statements submitted for tax filing purposes.

This non-compliance is limited to the company’s domestic mainland China operations, and we did not identify any similar issues across its Hong Kong or Singapore regional offices during our review scope.

No additional unreported compliance gaps related to statutory benefits have been identified beyond the contribution base shortfalls documented in this finding.

Subject: Escalation: Unresolved Patent Infringement Litigation for FY24 Target Due Diligence

This message escalates a critical roadblock in the FY24 target company financial due diligence project related to an unresolved patent infringement lawsuit. As of April 12, 2026, the target has provided only two internal status updates and no supporting documentation from its legal counsel regarding potential financial liabilities.

The lawsuit was first filed in the Guangzhou Intermediate People’s Court in October 2024, alleging the target’s core product line infringes on a patented industrial automation component. The target’s initial response in December 2024 claimed the patent was invalid, but has not submitted formal legal filings or expert testimony to support this position as of 9M26.

Our team has verified that the alleged infringing component accounts for 22% of the target’s HK$1.2 billion annual revenue from automated equipment sales in FY25. If the court rules against the target in the upcoming July 2026 hearing, the company could face mandatory product redesign costs of up to RMB 85 million plus triple damages totaling HK$320 million as outlined in the plaintiff’s initial claim.

Current internal team projections show we cannot finalize the contingent liability disclosure section of the 9M26 due diligence report without formal legal opinion from the target’s retained counsel. We have sent two follow-up requests to the target’s legal team on March 28 and April 5, 2026, and have received no formal response as of this writing.

To resolve this block, we request the project’s lead partner to coordinate with the target’s lead investor to request expedited access to the target’s full legal file related to this litigation by April 22, 2026. This timeline will allow our team to complete the required risk assessment and include accurate contingent liability disclosures in the final report due on April 26, 2026.

We are available for a 15-minute sync at your convenience tomorrow to walk through additional details of the case and available supporting documents we have collected to date.

Subject: FY26 FDD Executive Summary: Impact of One-Time Government Grants on Recurring EBITDA

This FDD identifies that the target’s reported FY25 recurring EBITDA overstated RMB 12.8 million due to unadjusted one-time government grants. The target recorded two separate RMB 6.4 million grants in FY25, both classified as operating revenue under local accounting standards but not tied to core operational performance.

We confirmed that these grants were tied to one-time facility expansion milestones, not ongoing revenue generation, so they should be excluded from recurring EBITDA calculations per global private equity reporting guidelines. This adjustment reduces the target’s reported FY25 recurring EBITDA by 9.2% relative to the initial management-provided numbers, which did not exclude the grants.

For FY26F, the target’s management projections include an estimated RMB 10.5 million in similar one-time grants, which will again require exclusion from recurring EBITDA unless the grants are reclassified as non-operating one-time items. This will create a consistent 7-10% gap between reported and adjusted recurring EBITDA for the forecast period.

Subject: Caveat on R&D Capitalization Assessment for Target Company

This memo supplements the FY24 to 9M26 FDD deliverable issued on October 12, 2026, to clarify the scope of our work related to the target’s R&D capitalization practices. Over the past three weeks, our team has reviewed the target’s publicly disclosed financial statements, board meeting minutes from 12 scheduled sessions, and internal R&D expense tracking spreadsheets shared via the secure data room between July and September 2026.

We have not conducted on-site interviews with the target’s R&D department heads or reviewed unredacted internal project feasibility reports for three ongoing AI model development initiatives, code-named Alpha, Beta and Gamma. This exclusion was agreed upon in our engagement letter dated August 15, 2026, as the target classified these projects as confidential intellectual property prior to our formal kickoff.

Our analysis of the target’s capitalization policy shows that it adjusted the amortization period for approved R&D projects from 5 years in FY24 to 7 years in FY25 and 9M26, with a total capitalized R&D balance of RMB 128.7 million as of September 30, 2026. We verified the calculation of capitalized costs against the stated policy but did not validate the internal controls around project approval for capitalization.

The unexamined feasibility reports and R&D team insights could reveal material deviations from the stated capitalization criteria, such as underreported ongoing project costs or misclassified routine maintenance expenses as R&D spend. If such deviations exist, the reported RMB 128.7 million capitalized balance could be overstated by up to 15% based on industry benchmarks for similar AI development projects.

This caveat does not alter our initial conclusion that the target’s capitalization practices align with Chinese Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises, but it limits the scope of our assurance to the publicly available and shared documented data we reviewed. We will update this assessment if the target provides access to the restricted R&D materials within the next 10 business days.

Subject: Analysis of Accrued Expenses Write-off in FY25

The accrued expenses line item for our target client saw a significant downward trend in FY25, with a total write-off of RMB 12.8 million against the FY24 ending accrued balance of RMB 9.7 million. Unlike typical quarterly accrual adjustments, this write-off was concentrated in the final two months of the fiscal year, marking a clear inflection point from the steady monthly accrual pattern seen in the first 10 months of FY25.

This one-time reversal represents roughly 18% of the client’s reported operating expenses for FY25, and it followed a mid-year review that identified overaccruals across three operational departments. The team’s initial analysis shows the overaccruals stemmed from inconsistent vendor invoice matching policies, which led teams to accrue expenses based on estimated costs rather than confirmed vendor bills for most of FY25.

While the write-off has corrected the prior period’s overstated accrued liabilities, we should note that the underlying policy gap remains unaddressed as of the end of FY25. We plan to follow up with the client’s finance team next week to confirm the root cause timeline and request supporting vendor correspondence to validate the reversal amount.

Subject: FY26 9M26 Return Reserve Adjustment Documentation - Third Follow-Up

Dear Ms. Carter,

This is my third formal request for the FY26 9M26 return reserve adjustment documentation that we initially asked for on October 12, followed by a reminder on October 26. I know you likely have a heavy end-of-quarter workload, so I wanted to circle back with full context for this request.

As you may recall, our FDD team identified that the 9M26 customer return rate reached 7.2%, which is a 18% increase compared to the 6.1% return rate recorded in 9M25. This upward trend requires updated reserve calculations that align with the latest historical data and IFRS 15 requirements.

Our audit plan for the client’s FY26 interim statements is scheduled to kick off on November 10, just 12 business days from today, and this documentation is a mandatory supporting file for the inventory and revenue recognition testing procedures. Without the updated reserve data, we will not be able to finalize our testing for the return reserve line item.

If you are unable to locate the full adjusted reserve schedule by the end of this week, we can accept a preliminary breakdown of the top 10 high-value return SKUs along with the revised reserve percentage for each category as a temporary substitute, as long as you can confirm the final numbers will be shared by November 8.

I have attached a copy of our original data request for your reference, and I am available to hop on a 15-minute call tomorrow or Wednesday morning if you have any questions about the specific information we need. Please let me know how you would prefer to proceed.

Best regards,
Li Wei
Senior FDD Consultant

Subject: FY25-FY26 Revenue Recognition Cutoff Findings

This finding identifies a RMB 12.8 million overstatement of 9M26 revenue due to premature revenue recognition for three large service contracts. The contracts were finalized and signed in early October 2026, but the target company recorded the full contract value in September 2026, shifting approximately 42% of the quarterly revenue from FY26Q4 to FY26Q3.

We verified the discrepancy by cross-referencing the signed contract dates, invoice issuance records, and the company’s revenue recognition log for the third and fourth quarters of 2026. All three contracts explicitly state that service commencement is scheduled for October 15, 2026, and the target’s internal policy requires revenue to be recognized proportionally over the service period rather than at contract signing.

The impact is limited to the 9M26 unaudited interim financial statements shared with the FDD team on October 22, 2026, and does not include FY25 historical results or full-year FY26 projections. No additional adjustments have been identified beyond the identified RMB 12.8 million overstatement at this stage.

Subject: Alignment on Deferred Subscription Revenue Recognition for 9M26

Dear Team,

First, I want to restate the position your audit team shared during yesterday’s call: you believe all 9M26 annual subscription contracts signed after June 30, 2026 should recognize 100% of the upfront fee in the month of contract execution, rather than deferring the revenue over the contract term.

Based on our review of the client’s standard subscription agreements and ASC 606 implementation guidelines we shared last week, our team holds a different view. We have cross-checked 42 active annual subscription contracts signed between July 1 and September 30, 2026, and found that 38 of them include a 7-day cooling-off period that allows customers to cancel without penalty, which creates a variable consideration constraint under ASC 606-10-25-8.

For the 38 contracts with cooling-off periods, we calculated that the total upfront fee recognized prematurely under your proposed method would be approximately RMB 12.8 million, which accounts for 19% of the client’s total 9M26 subscription revenue reported in your draft audit working papers. This would result in a 12% overstatement of the client’s quarterly gross revenue if adjusted to our recommended deferral approach.

To resolve this discrepancy, we propose scheduling a 30-minute sync tomorrow afternoon to walk through the 5 sample contracts we selected for detailed testing, including the cooling-off period clause analysis and variable consideration calculation model we built.

We have attached a one-page summary of our analysis and the 5 sample contract excerpts for your reference ahead of the call, and we are happy to adjust our approach if you can provide additional guidance on how your team interprets the variable consideration rules for contracts with cancellation clauses.

Best regards,
Li Ming

Subject: Escalation: Fixed Asset Depreciation Life Change Impact on FY26 Q3 Profit

I am writing to escalate a critical roadblock encountered during the 9M26 financial data review for the ABC Group FDD engagement. The client has proposed adjusting the depreciation lives of their manufacturing equipment from 10 years to 15 years, which would reduce accumulated depreciation by RMB 8.7 million in the first nine months of 2026 and increase reported operating profit by 12.3% relative to the original forecast.

Our team has cross-checked the client’s supporting documents, including their internal equipment maintenance logs and industry benchmark reports, but we found no official regulatory guidance or precedent from the local tax bureau to validate this proposed change. We also confirmed that the client’s prior two fiscal years used the original 10-year depreciation policy, with no prior disclosure of planned useful life adjustments.

As of today, we have 12 business days remaining before the FY26 Q3 draft report deadline. Without a formal decision on whether to accept the client’s proposed adjustment, our team cannot finalize the profit reconciliation section or sign off on the 9M26 financial statements. We request that the project leadership team review this matter by EOD Thursday, October 10, and provide clear guidance on next steps.

Subject: Query on Accrued Expenses Reversal as of FY25 Year End

Dear Ms. Carter,

This email follows up on the FY25 financial statements we reviewed last week, where we identified a total reversal of RMB 8.2 million in accrued expenses during the final three days of FY25. Specifically, the reversal included RMB 3.1 million in contracted service fees, RMB 2.7 million in office rental accruals, and RMB 2.4 million in employee bonus provisions, which represented 41% of the total accrued expenses booked as of December 31, 2025.

To validate the appropriateness of this reversal, we request access to three specific supporting documents: the signed amendment to the Q4 2025 service contract dated December 29, 2025, the formal rental abatement notice issued by the property management company on December 30, 2025, and the approved FY25 bonus payout memo dated December 31, 2025. We also need a written breakdown of the timing and rationale for each line-item reversal prepared by your accounting team.

We understand that year-end closing processes often involve tight timelines, but this reversal represents a material adjustment to our FY25 working capital calculations. If we do not receive these documents by this Friday, March 15, we will have to proceed with our preliminary analysis based on the available public disclosures, which may require additional adjustment notes in the final FDD report.

Best regards,
Li Ming
Senior FDD Project Manager

Subject: Caveat on Social Insurance and Housing Fund Compliance Check for FY24-FY25

This memorandum outlines the scope and limitations of our social insurance and housing fund compliance review for the target company’s mainland China operations, conducted between October 2026 and early November 2026. We reviewed the target’s official payroll filings, annual social insurance declaration forms, and internal payroll summary reports for fiscal years 2024 and 2025, as well as 9 months of FY26 provisional payroll data. We cross-referenced these records with the local social security bureau’s public minimum contribution base for each reporting period, which was adjusted annually in July of each year.

We did not conduct full employee-level verification of actual cash compensation paid to each staff member, nor did we obtain original bank transfer records linking payroll disbursements to individual employee accounts. Additionally, we were unable to access the target’s HR system to cross-check headcount figures against payroll submissions, as the target’s IT team restricted remote access to the platform during our fieldwork.

For FY24, the local social security minimum contribution base was RMB 4,250 per month, and the target reported a total average contribution base of RMB 4,120 per employee per month, representing a 3.06% shortfall relative to the mandatory requirement. For FY25, the minimum base rose to RMB 4,680 per month, and the target’s reported average base was RMB 4,410, a 5.77% shortfall. For 9M26, the provisional average base was RMB 4,520, which falls below the newly adjusted FY26 minimum base of RMB 4,920 set in July 2026.

This compliance shortfall could create two key risks for the transaction. First, local tax and social security authorities may impose back payments of outstanding contributions plus late payment fees, which we estimate could total between RMB 1.2 million and RMB 1.8 million across the three reviewed periods. Second, the target’s potential exposure could impact the valuation of its mainland operating entity, as regulatory non-compliance may reduce the perceived stability of its ongoing operating costs.

We have not reviewed any social insurance or housing fund contributions for temporary contract workers or third-party contracted staff, as the target did not provide a breakdown of these workers’ payroll and contribution records during our review period. This omission means our analysis only covers the target’s full-time, directly employed staff, and may understate the full scope of potential compliance risks.

Please note that this analysis is not intended to serve as a formal legal opinion on the target’s compliance status, and all stakeholders should consult local legal and tax advisors for a full assessment of potential liabilities.

Subject: Key FDD Finding: One-Time Government Grants Misclassified in Recurring EBITDA

One-time FY24 government grants totaling RMB 12.8 million were incorrectly included in the target’s recurring EBITDA calculation for 9M26.

The target’s accounting team treated the ongoing operational subsidy tied to local talent retention as a permanent recurring revenue stream, rather than a one-time grant approved only for FY24 staff retention costs. We verified this by cross-referencing the original grant approval letter dated March 2024, which explicitly stated the funds were non-recurring and limited to that fiscal year. The team also failed to reverse the grant recognition in 9M26 after the FY24 reporting period closed.

This misclassification inflated the reported 9M26 recurring EBITDA by 8.2% relative to the audited pro forma adjustments we recommended in our initial draft report. It will directly impact the proposed earn-out structure tied to recurring EBITDA milestones for FY26F, as the target’s reported performance will overstate its baseline recurring profitability.

Subject: Follow-up on FY25 Working Capital Seasonal Adjustment Documentation

Dear Ms. Henderson,

This is the third formal request I have sent to your team regarding the detailed breakdown of FY25 working capital seasonal adjustments for our FDD engagement. We first raised this requirement in our 12 March 2026 audit kickoff memo, followed by a formal data request sent via our client portal on 21 April 2026, and a reminder email on 18 May 2026. To date, we have not received any structured documentation matching our requested scope.

The working capital seasonal adjustment analysis is a core component of our FY26 FDD deliverable, as it will be used to validate the sustainability of the client’s reported 9M26 operating cash flow margin of 8.2%. Without the detailed breakdown of monthly inventory swings, accounts receivable collection cycles and accounts payable payment terms across Q3 and Q4 FY25, we will be unable to finalize the working capital normalization schedule that forms the basis of our transaction fairness opinion.

As we are currently operating on a tight timeline for this engagement, with only 12 business days remaining until our 30 June 2026 submission deadline, this delay is beginning to impact our ability to deliver a fully vetted, error-free report to our client’s investment committee. We understand that your team may have competing priorities, but this data is critical to meeting our shared project milestones.

If your team is unable to pull the full detailed breakdown by 23 June 2026, we would like to propose an alternative: we can accept the consolidated FY25 working capital statement provided in your 10 April 2026 board pack, paired with a signed management representation letter confirming that the seasonal adjustments were calculated in line with GAAP and align with prior year trends. This alternative would allow us to move forward with our analysis without further delay.

Please confirm receipt of this request by end of day tomorrow, and let us know if you require additional context or support to access the requested documentation. We appreciate your prompt attention to this critical item.

Best regards,
Li Wei
FDD Engagement Lead

Subject: Dispute Note on Target’s Customer Concentration Risk

Dear Partner Team and External Advisors,

First, I would like to restate the core position our external consulting team has shared in our last two sync meetings: the target company’s customer concentration risk is currently within acceptable thresholds for the planned M&A transaction, based on the confirmed FY24 revenue breakdown and the signed 12-month extension offer from its top client.

We have reviewed the same FY24 financial statements and the 9M26 interim revenue data, which show that the top three clients contributed 78% and 82% of total revenue respectively, with the single largest client accounting for 42% of FY24 revenue and 45% of 9M26 revenue. Our team’s reading of these figures is that the over-reliance on a single customer has not been fully mitigated, even with the pending extension.

Our analysis is further supported by the standard FDD disclosure guidelines for mid-market M&A deals, which require explicit disclosure of customer concentration risks when a single client contributes more than 30% of annual revenue, regardless of existing contract renewals. The target’s largest client contract is set to expire at the end of FY26, and there is no formal written commitment for a renewal beyond that term.

To resolve this discrepancy, we propose that we jointly commission a third-party customer retention survey to assess the likelihood of the top client extending its contract post-FY26, and include a quantified risk adjustment in the transaction valuation model based on the survey results.

We welcome your feedback on this proposed next step, and are available to join a 30-minute sync call tomorrow afternoon to walk through our data and supporting documents if that would help align our teams.

Best regards,
FDD Project Lead Team

structure.why: 先完整复述对方观点，让对方确认我们准确理解了他们的立场，避免后续沟通出现误解，是分歧沟通的标准开篇步骤。

Subject: Query on Cross-border Settlement Exchange Rate Exposure for FY24-FY26

Dear Ms. Carter,

Following our review of the target company’s preliminary financial statements for 9M26, we identified a material discrepancy between the reported realized exchange gains/losses of RMB 12.8 million and the supporting settlement records we have received to date. Specifically, the submitted bank remittance slips only cover 62% of the total USD-denominated cross-border transactions recorded in the general ledger during the first nine months of 2026.

To resolve this inconsistency and complete our due diligence workpapers, we require you to provide the full set of exchange rate exposure management ledgers for FY24, FY25 and 9M26, along with matching wire transfer confirmations, forward contract statements and daily exchange rate snapshots used for valuation. Each document should be labeled with the transaction date, counterparty name and settlement currency to ensure traceability.

We understand your team has been managing multiple urgent year-end closing tasks, so we have prepared a standardized file folder template with clear naming conventions to help you organize the materials efficiently. Please share the completed package via our secure client portal by EOD this Wednesday, November 13, 2026, to avoid delaying the final audit report submission.

Best regards,
Liam Chen
Senior FDD Project Manager

Subject: FDD Finding: Change in Fixed Asset Depreciation Lives for FY24-FY25

This finding documents a 20% increase in reported operating profit for Target Co. in FY25 driven by an unapproved change to fixed asset depreciation lives. Specifically, the company extended the depreciation period for its core production equipment from 10 years to 12 years starting January 1, 2025, with no formal board approval or disclosure to external stakeholders.

We verified this change by cross-referencing the 2025 fixed asset depreciation schedule against the 2023 and 2024 audited financial statements. For the 1,200 units of core production equipment with a total gross book value of RMB 890 million, the annual depreciation expense decreased by RMB 17.8 million in FY25, directly lifting operating profit by the same amount. We also confirmed that no similar adjustment was made to other asset categories such as office equipment or vehicles.

The impact of this change is material relative to the target’s reported FY25 operating profit of RMB 890 million, representing a 2.0% upward distortion of the stated profitability. This adjustment also reverses a 1.5% downward profit impact recorded in FY24, when the company temporarily shortened depreciation lives for a 6-month trial period before rolling back the change without formal sign-off.

We limited our analysis to the core production equipment category identified in the company’s 2025 depreciation policy memo, and did not review changes to leasehold improvements or intangible asset amortization schedules. All supporting documentation was extracted from the target’s internal financial system and shared drive, with no third-party validation obtained beyond the provided internal records.

This finding does not include potential downstream impacts on deferred tax liabilities or working capital reserves, as those calculations require additional tax filing data that was not provided during the current phase of due diligence.

Subject: Analysis of Related Party Purchase Pricing for Target Co.

This memo summarizes key trends and anomalies in Target Co.’s related party procurement pricing over FY24 to 9M26, based on the internal purchase ledger data shared last week.

The most notable shift occurred between FY24 and FY25, when the proportion of purchases from related parties rose from 32% of total procurement spend to 47%, before falling back to 39% in the first nine months of 2026. This swing followed a 12% jump in the unit price paid to the largest related party supplier in FY25, which was not matched by any corresponding increase in market benchmark rates for the same raw materials.

Independent market surveys conducted by our third-party data provider show that the average market price for the core raw material used by Target Co. increased by just 4% in FY25 and a further 2% in 9M26. In contrast, the unit price paid to the related party supplier jumped 12% in FY25 and held steady at that elevated level through 9M26, creating a consistent 8-10% price gap between the related party rate and prevailing market rates.

This sustained price disparity has led to a cumulative overpayment of approximately RMB 12.8 million in FY25 and RMB 9.3 million in 9M26, based on our calculation of the difference between the related party pricing and the adjusted market benchmark rates. The overpayment amount accounts for roughly 2.1% of Target Co.’s reported operating profit for FY25, a material impact on its bottom line.

We have not yet received the full set of third-party bidding documents for the related party supplier contracts, but the consistent trend of misalignment between related party pricing and market rates warrants further review during the remaining phase of the FDD.

No additional adjustments to the target company’s normalized profit margins have been proposed at this stage, as we are still gathering supporting documentation to validate the full extent of the pricing discrepancy.

Subject: Follow-up on Third-Party Pricing Documentation for FY26 Related Party Procurement

Dear Ms. Carter,

This is the third formal follow-up email I have sent regarding the third-party pricing comparison documents for the FY26 related party procurement transactions with XYZ Industrial Co., Ltd., which we first requested on September 12, 2025, and followed up again on October 3, 2025.

As of today, October 17, 2025, we have not received any draft or final version of the required materials, despite two prior reminders and a 35-day window for preparation since our initial request. This delay has started to create measurable bottlenecks in our FDD workstream, as our team needs to cross-reference the pricing against market benchmarks to validate the arm’s length nature of the transactions.

Our internal timeline for the FY26 FDD project requires that all core documentation, including this pricing package, be submitted by October 29, 2025, to allow for two weeks of cross-checking and audit adjustment preparation before our on-site fieldwork begins on November 10, 2025.

If the full set of third-party pricing comparisons is not available by the deadline, we can accept a provisional summary of the approved pricing thresholds and the list of comparable third-party vendors used for the 2025 procurement cycles, as a temporary workaround to keep the project on track.

Please confirm receipt of this email by end of day October 18, 2025, and let us know a firm date by which you can either share the full documentation or confirm the provisional alternative materials. If you are facing internal barriers to accessing the files, we are happy to schedule a 15-minute sync tomorrow to troubleshoot the process together.

Best regards,
Li Ming
FDD Project Associate
China Capital Advisory

Subject: Query on Inventory Impairment Provision for FY25 and 9M26

Dear Ms. Carter,

This email follows up on our ongoing financial due diligence for the acquisition of Brightway Manufacturing, and we are writing to flag inconsistencies identified in your team’s reported inventory impairment provision balances for FY25 and the first nine months of 2026.

Based on our review of your public quarterly filings and on-site inventory sampling completed last week, we noted that your reported total inventory impairment provision for 9M26 is RMB 12.8 million, which is 37% lower than the RMB 20.3 million provision recorded for the same period in FY24, even though your reported ending inventory balance for 9M26 has risen by 22% to RMB 417.6 million compared to FY24’s 9M end balance of RMB 342.5 million.

We have cross-referenced your disclosed sales slowdown data for low-margin custom component lines, which saw a 29% year-over-year decline in 9M26, and observed that 18% of your finished goods inventory consists of components that have not been shipped for more than 12 months, per our warehouse walkthrough documentation. None of these high-risk inventory lines were included in your current impairment provision calculation.

To resolve these discrepancies, we request that your team provide the full inventory impairment provision working papers for FY25 and 9M26 by close of business on Friday, October 18, 2026. Specifically, we need copies of the detailed aging schedule for slow-moving inventory, the market price benchmarks used to calculate net realizable value, and the approval records for the 2026 impairment provision setup.

We understand that compiling this documentation may require additional effort from your team, and we are available to walk through our sampling results or clarify any questions you may have by phone or in-person meeting tomorrow. Please let us know if you need additional support to meet the requested deadline.

Best regards,
Li Ming
FDD Project Lead
East Asia Capital Partners

Subject: Analysis of 9M26 Customer Return Rate and Related Allowance Balance

The 9-month 2026 customer return rate for the target’s core consumer electronics line has shown a clear upward trend that deviates from historical patterns. Over the same 9-month period across 2024 and 2025, the quarterly average return rate stayed within a narrow band of 3.2% to 3.8%, with minimal quarter-over-quarter fluctuations. However, the cumulative return rate for 9M26 already hit 5.7% as of the end of September, marking a 50% increase compared to the prior year’s full-year average of 3.9%.

This upward shift is not driven by a single off-cycle batch of returns, but rather a consistent monthly increase since March 2026. Each month from March through August 2026, the return rate rose incrementally, jumping from 4.1% in March to 6.3% in August before a slight dip to 5.9% in September. This steady climb suggests a systemic shift in the target’s product quality or customer return policies, rather than one-time operational errors.

The target’s recorded sales return allowance balance as of September 30, 2026, was RMB 12.8 million, which matches the balance carried at the end of 9M25. No incremental allowance has been booked to account for the higher current-year return rate. For context, the 2025 full-year return rate of 3.9% would have justified an allowance balance of roughly RMB 11.2 million based on the 9M26 total sales revenue of RMB 287 million.

Using the current 9M26 cumulative return rate of 5.7% as a proxy for full-year 2026 performance, the required ending allowance balance would increase to approximately RMB 16.3 million. This represents a RMB 3.5 million shortfall relative to the currently reported balance, which would directly reduce reported operating profit for the full year 2026 by a comparable margin.

Even if the September dip signals a temporary slowdown in return growth, the gap between actual return activity and the recorded allowance remains significant. The target’s finance team has not provided any documentation explaining why the allowance balance was not adjusted upward alongside the rising return rate, leaving this discrepancy unresolved for the final FDD report.

This analysis highlights a material inconsistency between the target’s reported financial reserves and the real-world return trends observed in 9M26, which warrants further investigation before finalizing the purchase price allocation and forecasted financials.

Subject: FDD Finding: Unresolved Product Liability Lawsuit for Target Co.

This finding relates to a pending product liability lawsuit against the target company, which was filed in October 2025. The plaintiff is seeking total damages of RMB 12.8 million, including lost profits, punitive damages and legal fees. Based on our review of the case filings and management’s internal risk assessment, the company has recorded a contingent liability of RMB 2.1 million in its FY25 financial statements, which is 16% of the claimed total amount.

We obtained the full case docket from the local court portal and reviewed 12 pages of supporting evidence submitted by both parties, including product testing reports from a third-party lab and internal quality control logs from Q3 2024 to Q2 2026. The target’s legal team has advised that the case is currently in the discovery phase, with a preliminary trial scheduled for mid-January 2027, and that the likelihood of a full payout of the claimed amount is assessed as less than 30% by external counsel.

This contingent liability only applies to the specific product line affected by the lawsuit, which accounts for 8% of the target’s total FY25 revenue. It does not include any potential follow-on claims from related customers, as we have not received additional complaint records beyond the case filings provided by the company.

Subject: Caveat on Social Insurance and Housing Fund Compliance for FY24-FY25

This caveat applies to all findings related to social insurance and housing fund disclosure in the FY24-FY25 financial due diligence deliverables. We conducted a line-item review of the client’s statutory contribution records for 12 months ending June 30, 2025, cross-referencing reported base salaries with monthly deduction slips from the company’s public bank accounts.

We verified that 92% of the 1,247 active employees on payroll had their social insurance and housing fund contributions calculated using their reported monthly base salary as the contribution base. For the remaining 8% of staff, we identified that 37 employees had contributions based on a capped amount of RMB 36,540 per month, which aligns with local 2025 statutory upper limits for first-tier cities.

However, we did not conduct verification of the actual total annual compensation for these employees, nor did we cross-reference contribution records with personal income tax filings or third-party payroll service reports. This is because the client’s internal payroll team was unable to provide complete historical compensation breakdowns for individual staff members outside of their formal base salary records.

This incomplete verification creates a potential gap in our assessment: we cannot confirm whether the client has fully complied with local regulations requiring contributions to be based on 100% of an employee’s total annual compensation, including bonuses and allowances. For the 37 employees identified with capped contributions, this gap means we cannot rule out the possibility of underreported total compensation and corresponding underpayment of statutory contributions.

We recommend that the client’s HR and finance teams conduct a full compensation breakdown review for the identified staff groups before finalizing any public disclosures related to statutory compliance. This caveat is not intended to question the client’s overall compliance posture, but to clarify the limited scope of our due diligence work.

Subject: Escalation: Non-compliant Social Security & Housing Fund Contribution Bases for FY25 Client

Dear [Project Lead & Partner],

This memo escalates a critical compliance check blockage identified during the 9M26 financial due diligence for our FY25 manufacturing client. Over the past 8 working days, our team has cross-referenced 127 payroll records against the local social security bureau’s official base thresholds, and found that 42% of frontline production staff’s contributions were calculated using a base 32% below the mandatory minimum for their job tier.

We have attempted to follow up with the client’s HR department three times via scheduled calls and formal email requests, but have only received partial, redacted payroll summaries that omit the key monthly salary breakdowns needed to verify the actual contribution base alignment. No timeline for full documentation has been provided, and delaying the final report beyond the 7-working-day deadline will trigger a 5% penalty fee per the client’s engagement letter.

We request that you coordinate with the client’s account manager to schedule a mandatory sync meeting within 24 hours to clarify the required documentation timeline, or approve a formal scope adjustment to include a qualified local compliance consultant to validate the reported discrepancy and calculate the estimated backpayment amount of approximately RMB 1.28 million.

Best regards,
[Your Full Name]
Senior FDD Consultant

Subject: FDD Execution Summary for Target Co. - FY26Q3 Revenue Inflation Risk

The core finding of our FY26Q3 financial due diligence is that the target’s reported Q3 revenue is inflated by approximately RMB 128 million due to forced dealer channel stuffing.

We identified this issue by cross-referencing the target’s monthly sales data, dealer inventory reports and third-party logistics records for the three months ended September 30, 2026. For the top 12 core distributors, which account for 68% of total reported Q3 revenue, the target’s sales volume in September 2026 was 42% higher than the average monthly sales volume from April to August 2026. Meanwhile, the total inventory held by these 12 distributors at the end of September 2026 increased by RMB 97 million compared to the end of August 2026, which is 76% of the reported incremental revenue from August to September.

Most of the additional inventory shipped to these core dealers in September was not supported by confirmed end-customer purchase orders, as documented in our follow-up checks with the target’s sales operations team. The target’s sales team offered extended 60-day payment terms and a 3% volume discount for dealers who accepted the extra stock in September, a promotion that was not offered in any prior month of FY26.

This channel stuffing will lead to underreported revenue in the first two quarters of FY27, as dealers will delay placing new orders until they work down the excess inventory accumulated in September 2026. Based on the inventory turnover rate of the top distributors, we estimate that the excess stock will take 5 to 7 months to clear, which will reduce projected FY27 Q1 and Q2 revenue by an estimated RMB 85 million to RMB 102 million combined.

We have not yet received confirmation from the target’s management on their plan to adjust the reported Q3 revenue or disclose this channel stuffing issue to potential investors, but we have flagged this risk in our preliminary due diligence report.

Subject: FY24 Supplier Rebate Accounting Treatment Dispute

Dear Team and External Auditors,

First, I want to restate your team’s confirmed position on the FY24 supplier rebate accounting: you believe all volume-based rebates received from CoreParts Ltd. in 9M24 should be recognized as a reduction of cost of goods sold in the same reporting period, with no deferral to future fiscal years.

Our team’s analysis is based on the detailed terms of the rebate agreement signed in January 2024, which states that rebates tied to annual cumulative order volume will only be paid after the full FY24 order target is met by March 31, 2025. We have verified that CoreParts only remitted RMB 1.28 million in rebates in October 2024, which covers only 72% of the projected annual rebate based on 9M24 order data, so we argue that partial rebates should be deferred until the full annual target is confirmed.

To align our views quickly, we propose exchanging the full 9M24 to 12M24 order records and the finalized rebate calculation sheet by this Wednesday, and schedule a 30-minute sync call on Thursday morning to review the remaining disputed items. We believe this step will help us narrow the gap without delaying the FY26 audit preparation timeline.

Best regards,
FDD Project Team

Subject: Valuation Adjustment Update for FY26 Target Due to Top Customer Contract Expiry

This memo outlines the required valuation adjustments tied to the pending expiration of the target’s top customer contract, which contributed 38% of the company’s FY24 operating revenue. First, we classify this adjustment as a revenue sustainability risk adjustment, as the contract with ABC Manufacturing — the single largest client — will terminate on 30 June 2026 with no confirmed renewal offer as of 15 March 2026.

We have quantified the impact using the target’s current trailing twelve-month (TTM) EBITDA multiple of 6.2x, which was agreed during the initial term sheet phase. The annualized revenue loss from the lost contract is approximately RMB 127 million, translating to a direct EBITDA reduction of RMB 31.8 million based on the target’s historical gross margin of 72% and SG&A allocation of 48% of gross profit. This equals a total equity value reduction of RMB 197 million before adjusting for debt-like items.

A critical second-order risk we identified is the accrued contract retention payment that is recorded as a current liability on the target’s 9M26 balance sheet. The target’s standard contract terms require a one-time retention payment of 5% of total contract value if the client terminates early, but in this case, the payment is due regardless of renewal status as the contract reaches its natural end. As of 15 March 2026, this accrued liability totals RMB 6.35 million, which has not yet been paid and must be deducted from enterprise value when calculating equity value to avoid double-counting the payment.

We have prepared a draft adjusted valuation model that incorporates both the revenue loss and the accrued liability adjustment, and we have cross-referenced the calculations against the target’s audited FY24 financial statements and 9M26 interim reports. We request that the deal lead circulate this memo to the legal team to confirm the exact payment terms of the ABC Manufacturing contract, and to schedule a 30-minute sync on 17 March 2026 to finalize the adjustment assumptions.

Subject: FY25 Revenue Adjustment for Dealer Channel Stock Build

This adjustment relates to the RMB 12.8 million overstated revenue in 9M26 caused by 3 key auto dealers holding excess inventory at quarter-end. As per our channel audit, these dealers were offered 15% volume discounts to stock 20% more units than their contracted monthly targets, with no enforceable commitment to resell the units within the standard 60-day return window.

We calculated the net valuation impact by reversing the recognized revenue and adjusting gross profit downward by RMB 2.1 million, which translates to a 3.2% reduction in FY25 adjusted EBITDA and a RMB 16.5 million decrease in enterprise value using the 5.2x FY25F EBITDA multiple applied to our target portfolio.

Critical risk to flag: the RMB 12.8 million receivable from these dealers remains recorded on the target’s balance sheet as of 30 September 2026, with no corresponding refund liability or inventory return reserve booked. If the receivable is not collected or the inventory is returned, we will need to reverse the full adjustment and adjust the equity bridge accordingly.

Next steps include requesting the target’s sales team to confirm the return terms of the excess inventory by end of day tomorrow, and updating the valuation model to reflect the contingent liability risk in the sensitivity analysis.

Subject: FY26 Target Company Valuation Adjustment for One-Time Government Grants

This memo outlines the required adjustment to the FY26F valuation model related to the RMB 12.8 million one-time technology upgrade grant received by the target in FY25.

First, this grant falls under the category of non-recurring income that was incorrectly included in the target’s reported EBITDA for FY25. Per the adjusted trading multiples benchmark, the target’s peer group uses recurring EBITDA as the core valuation metric, excluding all one-time government subsidies unrelated to core operations.

Based on the peer median multiple of 7.2x trailing 12-month recurring EBITDA, the RMB 12.8 million grant will reduce the reported FY25 EBITDA by the same amount, leading to a total downward valuation adjustment of RMB 92.16 million before accounting for debt-like items.

A critical secondary risk to flag is that the grant has not yet been fully disbursed: as of the end of 9M26, RMB 4.2 million of the total grant remains recorded as accounts receivable on the target’s balance sheet, rather than being classified as a debt-like item to be deducted from enterprise value when calculating equity value.

If the remaining grant funds are not received by the end of FY26, the receivable balance will need to be classified as a debt-like adjustment, which would further reduce the final equity value by the outstanding RMB 4.2 million. Moving forward, the finance team will confirm the final disbursement timeline of the grant by October 15, 2026, to finalize the valuation model adjustments.

We will circulate the revised model draft with full breakdowns of the EBITDA adjustment and debt-like item treatment by close of business tomorrow for your review.

Subject: FY25 Valuation Adjustment: Supplier Rebate Accounting Treatment

This memo outlines the required adjustment for the target’s FY25 supplier rebate accounting, which was identified during our FDD fieldwork. The target recognizes rebate income only when cash is received, rather than accruing it when the rebate eligibility is confirmed per contractual terms. For FY25, we calculated the accrued but unrecorded rebate liability at RMB 12.8 million, based on 9M25 settlement data and annualized quarterly purchase volumes.

The adjustment will reduce the target’s reported EBITDA by RMB 12.8 million for FY25, translating to a 0.7x downward shift in the EV/EBITDA multiple if we apply the 18x industry benchmark. This is a core operating adjustment, as it corrects the mismatch between revenue recognition and the actual economic benefit of rebate programs.

Critical note: As of the valuation date, the target has not settled RMB 8.3 million of the accrued rebate liability, which remains classified as accounts payable on its balance sheet. This means the item is a debt-like adjustment that must be deducted from enterprise value when calculating equity value, otherwise we will overstate the equity transfer value by double-counting the rebate benefit.

Next steps: I will share the full breakdown of the 9M25 rebate calculation by EOD tomorrow, and coordinate with the target’s finance team to confirm the remaining unpaid balance by this Friday.

Subject: Valuation Adjustment for Target’s FY26 Contingent Litigation Liability

This memo outlines the valuation adjustment required for the pending product liability lawsuit against Target Co., which was identified during our FDD fieldwork in 9M26. The lawsuit, filed by a major retail partner in March 2025, alleges breach of supply chain terms and seeks RMB 128 million in compensatory damages plus accrued interest. Our initial assessment confirms this qualifies as a recognized contingent liability under IFRS 15, as the likelihood of a unfavorable ruling is assessed at 65% based on external counsel’s updated opinion.

We have quantified the adjustment impact using the target’s existing EV/EBITDA multiple of 8.2x applied to the adjusted EBITDA for FY26F. The base case adjustment of RMB 128 million directly reduces the enterprise value by the full claim amount, resulting in a downward valuation shift of RMB 128 million, or approximately USD 17.6 million at the current 7.25 RMB/USD exchange rate. For context, this adjustment represents 3.2% of the target’s reported FY25 EBITDA of RMB 3.98 billion.

A critical secondary risk associated with this adjustment is the off-balance sheet debt-like exposure that has not yet been recorded in the target’s books. As of the end of 9M26, the target has not accrued any reserve for this lawsuit, meaning the full RMB 128 million claim would be treated as a debt-like item if a settlement is reached prior to closing. If we fail to account for this and include the adjustment in the equity bridge, we would inadvertently double-count the liability, leading to an overstated purchase price for the buyer.

We have coordinated with the target’s in-house legal team to request a formal written confirmation of the accrued reserve status by the end of this week, and will follow up with our external counsel to review the latest court filing dated October 12, 2026. Additionally, we will draft a standard purchase agreement indemnification clause to allocate any potential settlement costs between the buyer and seller if the case proceeds to trial after closing.
